facts.note: 31.3% of the book. Was 0.2% of total loans in March 2025 on the MHCLG return.

summary.text:
A refinancing concentration rather than a rate problem. Of a £687.5m book, 41 PWLB loans totalling £205m mature before 31 March 2028 at an average 4.73%, and alongside them sit £40m of LOBOs callable within twelve months which the council says it would repay rather than reprice. Roughly £245m therefore resets inside two years.

Short-term borrowing has grown from almost nothing to £215.5m, about a third of the book; across the 171 authorities with loan books over £250m the typical share at the last published return was around 2%. Table 1 also shows the council over-borrowed by £61.9m at 31 March against a strategy that assumed £2.6m of internal borrowing.

Two £5m five-year loans settled on 31 July at 5.46% and 5.44%, priced on 23 and 24 July — both reproduced exactly from our series, and both after the Q1 report closed, so they appear in no committee paper yet. They look like the short-versus-long review the Q1 report says was under way with Arlingclose.

status.note: Three named contacts with addresses. Anchored on Audit Committee, 10 September.

officer.subject: £245m of your borrowing reprices before 2028
officer.body:
Hi all,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, and every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts ahead of your Audit Committee on 10 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your Q1 report is clear and well laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The market has changed its mind since February. PWLB rates are roughly 0.6% higher than when your strategy went to Full Council on 25 February, and Bank Rate — 3.75% today — is now priced to rise to about 4.1% within a year rather than fall. As a cross-check that our numbers tie to yours: paragraph 5.6.3 gives the five-year certainty rate as 5.07% at the end of Q1, and our series gives 5.07% for the same day.

You've started terming out, and we can see it. Through March you drew six £5m loans, all maturing inside 2027, at 4.69-4.76%. On 31 July two more settled — both £5m, both five-year, at 5.46% and 5.44% on the Certainty Rate, priced on 23 and 24 July. That looks like the short-versus-long review your Q1 report says was under way with Arlingclose, and it happened after the report closed, so it isn't in any paper yet.

That timing matters for Medway more than most. We hold all 99 of your PWLB loans — £521.02m, matching your own Table 3A — at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Of those, 41 loans totalling £205m mature before 31 March 2028 at an average 4.73%, and alongside them sits the £40m of callable LOBOs at paragraph 5.6.12. Short-term borrowing now stands at £215.5m, roughly a third of the book; across the 171 authorities with loan books over £250m the typical share at the last published return was around 2%.

Which is why I'd point you to the monthly sector data at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. July's is up: £368m drawn across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers, average 5.02%, after the thinnest May in years — so you can see whether the market is thinning or reopening before you roll, not after.

None of it needs a meeting or a subscription, and the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check. On training, four look most relevant to Medway: LOBO loans, for the £40m callable inside twelve months; Interest rate risk, for the short-term third of the book; Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the £205m maturing before 2028; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this report goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
